lessons.title: What Section 80C Is and Who Can Claim It

children.text: Every January, HR teams across India send the same email: submit your investment proofs. Suddenly your WhatsApp groups fill up with ELSS tips, an uncle recommends an endowment policy, and a colleague swears by PPF. All of this frenzy traces back to one provision in the income tax law. Before you spend a single rupee on it, you need to understand what it actually does and whether it even applies to you.

Section 80C lets you subtract money you have put into specified investments and paid towards specified expenses from your income before tax is calculated. PPF deposits, ELSS mutual funds, your EPF contribution, life insurance premiums, your children's tuition fees and the principal part of your home loan EMI all qualify. The combined cap is ₹1,50,000 in a year.

body.text: Section 80C does not reduce your tax. It reduces the income your tax is calculated on. How much you actually save depends entirely on your slab.

body.caption: A deduction works on the income side of the calculation, before slab rates are applied.

body.text: New law, same idea. From 1 April 2026, the Income-tax Act, 2025 replaced the Income-tax Act, 1961. The old Section 80C is now Section 123 of the new Act, and the list of eligible investments and payments sits in Schedule XV. The ₹1,50,000 limit is unchanged. The new Act also uses a single term, 'tax year', in place of the old 'previous year' and 'assessment year'. In this course we cite Section 123 (80C) because '80C' is still what you will see on payslips, investment declaration portals and fund house marketing.

body.title: Quick Check: The New Section Number
body.textWithBlank: Under the Income-tax Act, 2025, the deduction formerly known as Section 80C is now Section ___.
body.explanation: Section 123 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 replaces Section 80C of the 1961 Act, with eligible items listed in Schedule XV. The ₹1,50,000 cap carries over unchanged.

children.text: A Worked Example: Rohan in Pune

Rohan is a software engineer in Pune earning ₹12,00,000 a year. He has opted for the old tax regime and claims the old-regime standard deduction of ₹50,000. Watch what happens when he uses the full ₹1,50,000 under Section 123 (80C).

body.caption: Rohan's tax under the old regime, with and without the full 80C deduction (surcharge not applicable at this income)

body.label: Rohan's tax saving
body.context: The ₹1,50,000 deduction came entirely out of his 30% slab: ₹45,000 in tax plus ₹1,800 in cess. The same ₹1,50,000 would save someone in the 5% slab only a fraction of this.

body.title: Your Turn: The 20% Slab
body.prompt: Meera, a bank officer in Kochi, is under the old regime. Her taxable income before 80C is ₹8,00,000. She invests ₹1,50,000 in PPF. The whole deduction falls in her 20% slab. How much tax does she save, including 4% cess?
body.explanation: ₹1,50,000 × 20% = ₹30,000 in tax. Add 4% cess: ₹30,000 × 1.04 = ₹31,200. Her taxable income drops from ₹8,00,000 to ₹6,50,000, still inside the ₹5 lakh to ₹10 lakh slab, so every rupee of the deduction was saved at 20%.

body.title: Eligibility Check
body.question: Which of these taxpayers can claim a deduction under Section 123 (80C)?
options: A private limited company that buys a keyman insurance policy
An HUF that deposits ₹1,00,000 into a PPF account opened before 2005
An LLP that invests its surplus in ELSS
A partnership firm that pays tuition fees for a partner's child
body.explanation: Only individuals and HUFs are eligible, so companies, LLPs and firms are out regardless of what they invest in. One nuance: HUFs have not been allowed to open new PPF accounts since 2005, but a pre-existing HUF PPF account can continue to receive deposits until maturity. For a new HUF investment, ELSS or life insurance on a member are the typical routes.

children.text: The Catch: It Only Works in the Old Regime

India runs two income tax regimes. The new regime, now Section 202 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (115BAC under the 1961 Act), is the default. It offers lower slab rates and a rebate that makes income up to ₹12 lakh tax-free, but it switches off almost every deduction, including Section 123 (80C). If you never actively choose the old regime, you are on the new one, and your 80C investments save you exactly zero rupees in tax.

body.text: Investing ₹1,50,000 in a five-year tax saver FD or a 20-year insurance policy 'to save tax' while you are on the new regime is the costliest version of this mistake. You lock up money, often at poor returns, for a benefit you are not receiving. Confirm your regime first. The companion course Old Tax Regime vs New Tax Regime covers how to decide.

body.title: Regime Check
body.question: Sneha, a marketing manager in Gurugram, never submitted a regime choice to her employer. In March she invests ₹1,50,000 in an ELSS fund through Zerodha Coin. How much deduction can she claim under Section 123 (80C) for that year?
options: ₹1,50,000, because ELSS is an eligible investment
₹75,000, because the new regime allows half
Zero, because she is on the default new regime
body.explanation: The new regime is the default. Since Sneha did not opt for the old regime, Section 123 (80C) is unavailable to her. Salaried taxpayers can still choose the old regime while filing their return, but only if the old regime actually works out cheaper once all their deductions are counted.

children.text: Deduction, Exemption, Rebate: Get the Words Right
People use these three words interchangeably. They are not the same thing, and mixing them up leads to wrong calculations. Flip through these before moving on.

cards.definition: An amount subtracted from gross total income to arrive at taxable income. Section 123 (80C) is a deduction. Its value to you depends on your slab.
Income that is never counted in your taxable income at all, such as HRA within limits or PPF maturity proceeds.
A reduction applied to the tax amount itself after slab rates are applied. It makes income up to ₹12 lakh tax-free under the new regime and up to ₹5 lakh under the old regime.
Your total income from all heads (salary, house property, business, capital gains, other sources) before deductions such as Section 123 (80C) are subtracted.
The 12-month period from 1 April to 31 March used under the Income-tax Act, 2025. It replaces the old 'previous year' and 'assessment year' pair.
The schedule to the Income-tax Act, 2025 that lists the investments and payments eligible for the Section 123 deduction.

body.title: Scenario: The First Payslip
body.scenario: Karthik, 23, just joined an IT services company in Hyderabad at a salary of ₹6,50,000 a year. HR asks him to submit his tax regime choice and investment declaration. A senior colleague tells him to buy a ₹1,50,000-a-year endowment policy right away, saying 'otherwise you will lose money to tax'.
body.prompt: Should Karthik buy the policy to save tax? Work out his position under both regimes before answering.
body.modelAnswer: No. Under the new regime, his salary after the ₹75,000 standard deduction is ₹5,75,000. That is well below ₹12 lakh, so the rebate brings his tax to zero with no investment required. Under the old regime, his salary after the ₹50,000 standard deduction is ₹6,00,000, and a full ₹1,50,000 80C claim would bring taxable income to ₹4,50,000. That falls under the ₹5 lakh old-regime rebate, which also means zero tax, but only after locking up ₹1,50,000 every year. The new regime gets him to zero tax for free, so there is no tax case for the policy. If he wants to save, he should pick products based on goals, returns and liquidity, and buy term insurance only if someone depends on his income.

events.title: Section 80C introduced
events.description: The Finance Act, 2005 brought in Section 80C with a ₹1,00,000 limit, replacing the older Section 88 tax rebate on savings.

events.title: Limit raised to ₹1.5 lakh
events.description: The Union Budget raised the 80C limit from ₹1,00,000 to ₹1,50,000. It has not changed since.

events.title: New regime introduced
events.description: Section 115BAC offered lower slab rates in exchange for giving up most deductions, including 80C. It was optional at the time.

events.title: New regime becomes default
events.description: From FY 2023-24, taxpayers were placed on the new regime unless they opted out, sharply reducing the reach of 80C.

events.title: ₹12 lakh rebate announced
events.description: The Union Budget raised the new-regime rebate so income up to ₹12 lakh is tax-free, pushing even more salaried taxpayers away from the old regime.

events.title: Income-tax Act, 2025 takes effect
events.description: Section 80C becomes Section 123 with Schedule XV. The ₹1,50,000 limit and old-regime-only status carry over.

body.title: Before You Invest a Rupee for 80C
steps: Confirm which tax regime you have declared to your employer (or plan to choose while filing)
Check your payslip for your own EPF contribution. It already counts towards the ₹1,50,000.
Add up existing eligible payments: life insurance premiums, children's tuition fees, home loan principal
Subtract that total from ₹1,50,000 to find your actual remaining 80C gap
Identify your marginal slab so you know what each ₹1 of deduction is really worth
Only then choose a product for the gap, based on your goals and lock-in comfort

body.label: Income Tax Department: Tax Calculator
body.description: Compare your tax under the old and new regimes on the official e-filing portal before you commit money to any 80C product.

points: Section 80C of the 1961 Act is Section 123 of the Income-tax Act, 2025, with eligible items listed in Schedule XV.
It is a deduction: it lowers taxable income by up to ₹1,50,000 a year, and the tax you save depends on your slab.
At the 30% slab, the full deduction saves up to ₹46,800 including cess. At 20% it saves ₹31,200.
Only individuals and HUFs can claim it. Companies, firms and LLPs cannot.
It works only under the old regime. On the default new regime, 80C investments give no tax benefit.
Count what already qualifies, such as EPF, insurance, tuition fees and home loan principal, before buying anything new.
